summary: Defines what an IPv6 node should support so devices can work well together across many kinds of deployments. It collects the requirements in one place for implementers. It is informational, replaces RFC 4294, and was in turn replaced by RFC 8504.

eli5.summary: A checklist for what any IPv6 device should be able to do, so devices from different makers can talk. It replaced an older checklist and later got a newer one itself.

questions: what does an ipv6 node need to support
how does ipv6 address autoconfiguration work
subtitle: A checklist of what IPv6 devices must support to work together.

tldr.problem: IPv6 will be deployed in many different devices and situations, but without a clear list of what every IPv6 node should implement, devices from different vendors may not interoperate well.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects and summarizes requirements from other published standards into one applicability statement, specifying which IPv6 specifications all nodes MUST or SHOULD implement for general use, while allowing specialized deployments to add stricter requirements.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6434 was replaced by RFC 8504, which updated the requirements to reflect advances in IPv6 deployment and changes to underlying standards since 2011.

today: RFC 6434 is an Informational document and has been obsoleted by RFC 8504, which provides an updated set of IPv6 node requirements reflecting changes in IPv6 deployment experience and underlying specifications since 2011. RFC 8504 remains the current applicability statement for IPv6 node requirements.

sections.title: Why Nodes Need Requirements
sections.content:
IPv6 is designed to work on many different kinds of devices and in many different deployment scenarios. To ensure that IPv6 works well and that devices can interoperate across these diverse situations, this RFC defines common functionality that all IPv6 nodes MUST support.

An IPv6 node is any device that implements IPv6. This includes both IPv6 hosts (devices that do not forward packets) and IPv6 routers (devices that do forward packets). This document covers both types and specifies a baseline of features so that nodes can reliably communicate.

The document is not a detailed protocol specification; rather, it is an applicability statement that references other RFCs. Different deployment scenarios may define stricter requirements or include optional features for specialized use. For example, the U.S. government and the Department of Defense have defined their own IPv6 profiles for their specific needs.
sections.eli5: IPv6 will run on many kinds of devices. This document says what features every device needs so they can all talk to each other, while allowing special devices to add more.

sections.title: Core IPv6 Protocol and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
All IPv6 nodes MUST support the Internet Protocol Version 6 (RFC 2460), including the ability to send, receive, and process IPv6 packets and fragment headers. Nodes MUST handle unrecognized extension headers as specified in RFC 2460. Special care is required for the Routing Header type 0 (RH0), which was deprecated due to security concerns and MUST be treated as an unrecognized routing type.

Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) is the IPv6 equivalent of ARP and is critical for finding neighbors on the same link. Hosts MUST support Router Discovery (finding routers), Prefix Discovery (learning which destinations are on-link), and Neighbor Unreachability Detection (NUD) to determine when neighbors have become unreachable. All nodes MUST respond to unicast Neighbor Solicitation messages. Hosts MUST support sending Router Solicitations and receiving Router Advertisements to learn about routers and address prefixes.

Nodes MUST support the sending and receiving of Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages, which are essential for Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) to ensure that addresses are not already in use on the link.
sections.eli5: Every IPv6 device needs the basic IPv6 protocol and Neighbor Discovery, which lets devices find each other on the same network segment.

sections.title: Address Configuration and DNS
sections.content:
All IPv6 nodes MUST support the IPv6 Addressing Architecture (RFC 4291) and handle multiple addresses simultaneously. Hosts MUST support IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862), which allows them to generate their own link-local and global addresses without any server. All nodes MUST implement Duplicate Address Detection to ensure addresses are not duplicated.

Hosts SHOULD implement the Privacy Extensions (RFC 4941) to protect user privacy by using temporary addresses that do not expose the device's globally unique interface identifier. All nodes MUST implement the Default Address Selection rules (RFC 3484) to correctly choose which address to use when a device has multiple configured addresses.

Hosts SHOULD implement DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) for stateful address configuration and other configuration parameters. While not required, DHCPv6 is essential in many deployment scenarios where per-device configuration is needed. All nodes SHOULD implement DNS stub resolver functionality (RFC 1034) with support for AAAA records, reverse address lookups via ip6.arpa, and EDNS0 to support larger DNS packets.
sections.eli5: Devices need ways to get or create IPv6 addresses and find other devices by name. Stateless autoconfiguration lets them do it themselves; DHCPv6 lets a server assign addresses; DNS lets them look up names.

sections.title: Upper Layer Protocols and ICMP
sections.content:
IPv6 nodes MUST support ICMPv6 (RFC 4443), which is the equivalent of IPv4's ICMP and is used for error reporting, path MTU discovery, and neighbor discovery. Nodes SHOULD support Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1981) to discover the largest packet size that can be transmitted on the path to a destination without needing fragmentation.

Nodes that need to receive multicast traffic MUST support Multicast Listener Discovery (MLDv1, RFC 2710). Nodes SHOULD implement either the full MLDv2 (RFC 3810) or Lightweight MLDv2 (RFC 5790) to support source-specific multicast, which allows applications to specify which senders they want to receive multicast data from.

The document references other specifications that define how IPv6 runs over various link layers (Ethernet, ATM, PPP, IEEE 802.15.4, etc.), noting that IPv6 may also be tunneled over other protocols like UDP for traversing Network Address Translators (Teredo, RFC 4380).
sections.eli5: Devices need ICMP for error messages and multicast support to join group communications. They should also handle different ways to carry IPv6 over various network technologies.

sections.title: Security, Mobility, and Management
sections.content:
The document notes that all IPv6 nodes face the same security challenges as other networked systems and should follow Jon Postel's Robustness Principle: be conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept. Security extensions such as IPsec (Encapsulating Security Payload and Authentication Header) are important but the RFC does not mandate specific implementations.

Implementations MAY support IP mobility (the ability to move between networks while maintaining connections), though this is optional for general nodes. Network Management via MIB (Management Information Base) modules MAY be implemented for systems that need to be managed remotely.

Routers have specific additional requirements including support for forwarding IPv6 packets, DHCPv6 relay functionality, and the IPv6 Router Alert Option. The RFC also notes that while IPv6 is designed for the future, some nodes MAY support IPv4 and transition mechanisms (RFC 4213) for coexistence during the transition period.
sections.eli5: Devices should be careful and defensive. Routers have extra jobs like forwarding. Some devices might support IPv4 too until IPv6 is everywhere. Mobility and management tools are optional.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
This RFC emphasizes that it defines minimal requirements for useful IPv6 service that apply across a broad range of device types and deployments. Specific deployment scenarios (government, enterprises, service providers) may define additional stricter requirements beyond what is specified here. The document is intended to provide guidance on which specifications should be implemented in the general case and which may be of interest only to specific deployment scenarios.

The granularity of requirements varies widely. While some RFCs define a single feature as a whole, many specifications define multiple independent pieces, some mandatory and some optional. Additionally, most specifications define both client and server roles, but implementations may focus on only one of those roles. Implementers should use this RFC as a starting point and then consult specific RFCs for details on what parts are actually required for their use case.
sections.eli5: This is a baseline. Real deployments might ask for more features depending on what the devices need to do. Implementers should read the referenced RFCs for details about what they actually need.

items.title: Router Discovery
items.text: Hosts learn which routers are on the link and can forward their packets to the wider network.

items.title: Prefix Discovery
items.text: Hosts learn which address prefixes are on-link and which require routing through a router.

items.title: Neighbor Unreachability Detection
items.text: Hosts detect when neighboring nodes have become unreachable and need to try alternate routes.

items.title: Duplicate Address Detection
items.text: All nodes verify that an address they want to use is not already in use by another device on the link.
